entries.modern_form: PIE *h₂m̥bʰi 'around, on both sides' (Pokorny 34 ambhi, m̥bhi; also *obhi, *ebhi) and the dual *h₂m̥bʰoh₁ 'both' (Pok. ambhō(u))
entries.note:
The root box is exactly Pokorny p.34 and Walde-Pokorny I 54-55: 'ambhi, m̥bhi "beiderseits wovon, um-herum" ... ambhō(u) Du. "beide", und ähnliche auf -bhi, -bho- ausgehende Formen', with the variants *obhi / *ebhi discussed in the same article ('setzt … sicher das idg. *obhi oder *ebhi fort'). Language label 'Indo-European' and both glosses ('around'; 'both') are right. Watkins/AHD has the same pair of entries, 'ambhi. Also mbhi. Around. Probably derived from ant-' and 'ambhō. Both', and Wiktionary reconstructs *h₂m̥bʰí (Jasanoff: from *h₂n̥t-bʰi, instr. pl. of *h₂ént-s 'forehead, front'; Dunkel: *án + *-bʰi) — i.e. modern work adds a pre-history for the root but does not challenge the shape or the meaning.

CROSS-CUTTING CAVEAT ON THE PERSIAN BRANCH. Nourai (following Horn 1893) files eight New Persian af-/f- verbs and nouns under Av. aiwi- (*abi-). Since Horn wrote, Persian af- has been shown to continue THREE distinct Old Iranian prefixes that all fall together in Middle Persian: *abi- (> MP ab-/awi-), *apa- 'away' and *upa-. Hübschmann already warned that Horn's nos. 102-106 are 'nicht einwandfrei, besonders der Bedeutung wegen' (HUB p.16-17), and Nyberg's Pahlavi glossary indexes afgandan, afsōs, afsūn, afsurdan under apa-, and afsar under *upa-sarah-. Nourai reproduces Horn's 1893 picture without those corrections, which is why five of the seven Iranian nodes below come out 'disputed'.

MIS-CITATION. Node #7 cites BQT:2143 for afšāndan/afšūn. Borhān-e Qāṭeʿ p.2143 (checked with tools/ref_page.py, vol.4 pdf p.226) is the نشان / نشاندن / نشاسته block, nothing to do with افشان; the real entries افشاندن / افشون stand in vol.1 at about p.150 (BQT_v1_pages.txt leaf 365).

nodes.words: aiwi, aibi, abi, aiwiš, ubě, uwa
nodes.derivation: Av. aiwi (Younger Avestan) / aibī (Gathic) 'to, against, over, in respect of' is the regular Iranian reflex of PIE *h₂m̥bʰi (or of the ablaut variant *obhi, which Pokorny and Kent think has fallen together with it in Indo-Iranian): PIE *m̥bʰi > Proto-Indo-Iranian *Habʰí > Skt. abhí, Av. aibī/aiwi. Before a following sibilant or in sandhi the preverb appears as aiwiš- (Av. aiwiš.hutəm 'pressed out', aiwiš.xᵛarəθa-), which is Nourai's 'aiwiš'. 'abi', however, is Old Persian abiy, not Avestan: Bartholomae's headword reads 'g. aibi, j. aiwi (aivi), p. abiy', so this Avestan box has one Old Persian form smuggled into it (Nourai repeats it correctly as its own node #12). ubě and uwa do not belong to the preposition at all but to the dual pronoun *h₂m̥bʰoh₁ 'both': Av. uwa- (masc.) / ubē (fem.) = Skt. ubhāu/ubhē, and Pokorny/Sommer explain the Indo-Iranian u- as a labial-conditioned darkening of *ambhāu > *abhāu. Grouping them under one heading is Pokorny's own arrangement, so this is a defensible chart, but the gloss 'over, above, both' is really two glosses for two different stems.

ref_check.note: POK_01.txt leaf 42: '*mbhi: ai. abhi-taḥ, av. aiwito "zu beiden Seiten, rings" (über av. aibis, apers. abis strittiger Bed. …); ai. abhi kann in der Bed. "um", apers. abiy, av. aibī, aiwi in der Bed. "über, in betreff von" aus *mbhi stammen'; and further down 'ai. ubhāu "beide", av. uwa- ds.'. Both halves of Nourai's node are on p.34; Pokorny too lists apers. abiy in the same breath, which is where Nourai's 'abi' comes from.

nodes.derivation: Four preverb compounds of aiwi-, of which only the first is actually attested. (a) aiwi-ruč = Av. aiwi.raocaya-, causative of raok-/raoč- 'to shine' (PIE *lewk-, Nourai's 'Leuk'), attested Vidēvdād 8.2 'aiiā dim aiwi.raocaiiāt āθrō' and V.19.33 'stārąm aiwi.raocaiiā̊nte', which Bartholomae renders 'mit aiwi: aufflammen lassen, entzünden an —'. (b) aiwi-reg is Horn's and Hübschmann's reconstruction Av. aiwi + razaiieiti 'ordnet, richtet' (root raz-, PIE *h₃reǵ-, Nourai's 'Reg'), not an attested compound; Hübschmann §93 states it explicitly ('zd. aiwi + razayeiti'). (c)/(d) aiwi-sāra- 'around the head' and aiwi-sara- 'on the head' are Horn's starred reconstructions (Horn nos. 97, 99 both print 'aw. *aiwisāra-' / 'aw. *aiwisara-' with an asterisk) built on sarah- 'head'; neither is in the Avesta, and the second is now generally replaced by *upa-sarah- (see node #3). Chart shows them as plain Avestan words with no asterisk, which over-states their status.

ref_check.note: Nourai gives no reference on this node; the forms are traceable to Horn nos. 93-99 and Hübschmann §93, checked under node #3.

nodes.derivation: Three of the four are sound, the fourth is now rejected. (a) afrūxtan افروختن 'to kindle, light up': Av. aiwi.raocaya- > MP abrōxtan/abrōz- (Book Pahlavi ʾplwhtn', ʾplwc-; Manichaean ʾbrwxt, ʾbrwc-) > NP afrōxtan/afrōz-; the -č- of raoč- gives MP/NP -z- in the present stem and -xt- in the past stem exactly as in sōxtan : sōz-. Confirmed. (b) afrāštan افراشتن 'to raise' (pres. afrāz-, whence the chart's extra افراز): Av. aiwi + raz- 'to make straight' (PIE *h₃reǵ-, cf. Lat. regō, Gk. ὀρέγω, Skt. irajyáti) > MP abrāstan/abrāz- (ʾplstn', ʾplc-; Man. ʾbrʾst), noun abrāz 'acclivity' > NP afrāz; Hübschmann adds that afrāstan is the original infinitive and afrāštan/afrāxtan the analogical remake after afrōz- : afrōxtan. Confirmed. (c) afsār افسار 'bridle, halter': MP *afsār (attested in the Bundahišn), borrowed early into Aramaic — Classical Syriac ʾap̄sārā, Jewish Babylonian Aramaic ʾap̄sārā/ʾap̄sīrā — which shows the word existed in Sasanian Persian; Horn's derivation from *aiwi-sāra- 'that which is round the head' is the classic one and nothing better has replaced it, but it is a starred form. Plausible. (d) afsar افسر 'crown' is DISPUTED: Hübschmann §99 backed *abisarah- (comparing Skt. abhiśiras-), but Henning (Selected Papers, 1977) ruled that afsar 'darf nicht auf *abisarah- (> *ōsar) zurückgeführt werden, vielleicht aber auf *upasarah-', and Nyberg's Pahlavi glossary follows him: 'api-sar [ʾpysl] crown … Probably < OIr *upa-sarah- "that which is on the head" > *apa-sara- and then remodelled to *api-sara- with variable accent: *ápi-sara- > *apsar > afsar'. So the sar 'head' element is right but the prefix is *upa-, and abi- is only a secondary re-formation — i.e. not Nourai's Ambhi at all, or only at one remove. (Nourai's second gloss for afsar, 'officer', is a modern 20th-c. army usage back-formed from afsar 'crown/insignia'; it is not an ancient meaning.)

nodes.derivation: (a) aiwi-saoka: this is Darmesteter's *aiwi-saoča- (Études iraniennes II 131), a compound of aiwi- with saoč-/saok- 'to burn' (PIE *(s)kewk-, Nourai's 'Keuk 1'), invented to explain afsōs. It is unattested and Horn demolished it on the spot: 'Darmesteter's Erklärung, Et. ir. II, 131 aus aw. *aiwisaoča- ist unhaltbar, da aw. č im Np. nicht zu s werden kann.' Nourai even prints it with -k- rather than Darmesteter's -č-. Disputed. (b) aiwi-kand: Horn no.103 already conceded 'Kaum etwas anderes als aw. aiwi + √kan-, wennschon die Bedeutung nicht passt', and modern Iranists have moved the prefix: Nyberg files MP apa-kandan '< OIr *apa-kan- and *upa-kan-', Cheung puts NP afgandan under '*kan¹ to throw, place, put' with '(+ *apa-)'. Disputed. (c) aiwi-zāvayeiti 'adds up' is the one solid member: it is really the Old Persian causative abiy-ajāvayam / abi-jāvayam (XPg 9, XPh 40) 'I added', from *abi- + gav-/zav- 'to procure, get' (PIE *gʰeu-/*gew-, Nourai's 'Geu 2'); Hübschmann §96 reconstructed *aiwi-zavayeiti in Avestan dress because Av. sav-/zav- and the SW-Iranian z- had to be reconciled. Confirmed as an etymon, but it is Old Persian rather than Avestan, and the box's language label is therefore loose.

ref_check.note: HUB.txt ff-leaf 26 (= printed p.16), no. 96: 'Aus aiwi + savayeiti wäre im Neup. *afsāyad geworden: das vorliegende afzāyad "vermehrt" muss auf *aiwizavayeiti zurückgehen' — this is precisely Nourai's third form, and Hübschmann's page 16 is the right citation for it. HUB p.16 says nothing about aiwi-saoka or aiwi-kand; on the very next page (p.17) Hübschmann adds 'Nr. 102-106 [= Horn's afšāndan, afgandan …]: Nicht einwandfrei, besonders der Bedeutung wegen.'

nodes.derivation: (a) afsūs افسوس (MP afsōs, Pāzand awasōs), older meaning 'mockery, scorn, jest' (Horn: 'Spott, Scherz'; MacKenzie: 'scorn, mockery'), only later 'alas, regret' — Nourai's gloss 'regret' is the modern sense only. Its etymology is genuinely open: Darmesteter's *aiwi-saoča- 'burning at' (DRM:131) is what Nourai draws, but Horn showed Av. č cannot yield NP s; Hübschmann §101 wrote 'Np. afsōs … wird auch von Fr. Müller nicht befriedigend erklärt'; Nyberg proposes apa-sōs '< OIr *apa-sraud- from apa + Av. srav- "to speak/hear"' (i.e. 'speaking against'). Disputed — modern scholarship does not accept the aiwi- + 'burn' route. (b) afkandan/afgandan افکندن 'to throw (away)': MP abgandan/abgan- (Book Pahlavi with the Aramaic ideogram LMYTWN-tn', Man. ʾbgnd, ʾbgn-) + NP -kandan from the root *kan 'to throw, dig'. The root is undisputed; the PREFIX is: Nyberg '< OIr *apa-kan- and *upa-kan-', Cheung '(+ *apa-)', Wiktionary '*Hápa "off, away" or *upó' — none of them *abi-, and the sense 'throw AWAY' fits apa- 'away' rather than abi- 'towards'. Disputed. (c) afzūdan افزودن 'to add, increase' (pres. afzāy-, noun afzūn فزون, the chart's extra): MP abzūdan/abzāy- (ʾpzwtn', ʾpzʾd-; Man. ʾbzʾy-), abzōn 'increase' > NP afzūn, from *abi-gav-/*abi-zav- 'to add to' — the very formation attested in Old Persian abiy-ajāvayam. Confirmed, and it is the one member of this node that really does descend from Ambhi.

ref_check.note: Not directly readable in DRM.txt (Darmesteter, Études iraniennes II p.131), but Horn quotes it verbatim on HRN p.23: 'Darmesteter's Erklärung, Et. ir. nodes.derivation: (a) aiwi-fšān: Horn no.102 offered 'aw. aiwi + fšūnayeinti "sie weiden aus", Yt 14,56 (?)' with his own question mark, and Hübschmann struck it out with nos.102-106 as 'nicht einwandfrei, besonders der Bedeutung wegen'. Modern Iranian etymology puts NP afšāndan under a root *šan 'to shake (down)' with the prefix *apa-: Cheung, EDIV s.v. *šan, '*MIDDLE PERSIAN: (+ *apa-) BMP ʾpsʾn- /afsan-/ "to spread, scatter, sow" … *NWIR: … (+ *apa-) NP afsandan/afsan-'. Neither the prefix nor the root shape (fšān vs šan) survives. Disputed. (b) aiwi-axš 'oversee' is genuine and well attested: Bartholomae lemmatises the verb 'āxš-, nur mit aiwi "ἐφορᾶν" [to oversee]. Präs. 30 (Iter.) aiwyāxšaya-. Inf. aiwyāxštriš', from aiwi- + axš-/haxš- 'to watch' (Nourai's 'Okw' = PIE *h₃ekʷ- 'to see'). Confirmed. Node verdict follows the weaker member.

nodes.derivation: afšāndan افشاندن 'to scatter, sprinkle' < MP afšāndan/afšān- (ʾpšʾn-tn'), pres. stem afšān-, whence the participial noun افشان 'scattering' used in compounds (آتش‌افشان, گل‌افشان; and the chart's Rumi line 'لب دُرفشانش' turns on that). afšūn افشون (also افشان) is the derived instrument noun: Moʿin, Farhang-e Fārsi, 'افشون [= افشان] (اِ.) افزاری است دارای پنجه‌ای چوبین (سه شاخه یا چهار شاخه) و دسته‌ای بلند که به وسیلهٔ آن غلهٔ کوفته را باد دهند و دانه را از کاه جدا سازند' — a long-handled three- or four-pronged wooden winnowing fork, so Nourai's gloss 'rake' is right. The word chain Persian ← Middle Persian is certain; what is disputed is the parent: the modern analysis is Old Iranian *apa-šan- 'to shake off/away' (Cheung; Wiktionary), not *aiwi-fšān-, and Horn's own citation of Yt 14.56 fšūnayeinti carried a question mark that Hübschmann converted into a rejection. Hence 'disputed' for the edge, not for the words.

nodes.derivation: Both compounds rest on segmenting the š of Persian šikār / šitāftan out of the preverb aiwiš-, and both segmentations have been abandoned. (a) aiwiš-kar: de Lagarde's and Horn's *aiwiš + kar-; but Horn himself refused Nourai's cross-reference to *kʷer- 'to make' — 'aber dann gewiss nicht zu √kar- "tun, machen", wie de Lagarde will, sondern zu √kar- in np. nigār, nigerīdan' — and Hübschmann analysed the doublet bišgard as bi-šgard < *vi-škart, i.e. the š- belongs to the STEM škar-. Cheung's EDIV settles it with a root '*skar "to pursue, drive, look for (the cattle)"' (MP škarag 'bird of prey', wiškar 'hunting-ground', Pth. ʾškr- 'to hunt', Sogd. škr-, Oss. skʼærun 'to chase animals'). Disputed. (b) aiwiš-tap: Horn no.777 derived šitāftan from 'aw. *aiwis + √tap-, tāpayeiti "in Wärme, Hitze bringen", dann tropisch'; but the Middle Persian form is awistāb-/ōštāb- (Man. ʾwystʾb-, BMP ʾwstʾp-), and Cheung files it under an independent root '*stap "to hasten, (op)press"' (PIE *step-, Pok. 1013; Arm. loanwords štapem, štap) with the prefix *abi- — so the preverb is indeed *abi-, but the š-t- is root-initial *st-, not aiwiš + t-. Disputed as segmented.

nodes.derivation: (a) šekār شکار 'hunt, game' with its verb šikardan, MP škar (Bundahišn glossary), wiškar 'hunting ground', škarag 'bird of prey', Parthian ʾškr- 'to hunt', Sogdian (ʾ)skr-/škr- 'to lead, pursue', Ossetic skʼærun 'to chase (animals)'. Modern Iranists (Cheung 2007: 345, followed by Wiktionary) derive the whole family from a root *skar 'to pursue, drive, look for (cattle)' with no preverb at all, and even suspect New Persian šikār of being a loan from Sogdian škʾr rather than an inherited SW-Iranian word, since MP has only the *wi- compound wiškar. Nourai's aiwiš-kar segmentation is therefore rejected. (b) šetāftan شتافتن 'to hurry' (pres. šitāb-, noun شتاب, the chart's extra) continues MP awistāftan > ōštāftan (Man. ʾwystʾb-, Book Pahlavi ʾwstʾp- 'to press, hasten'), from *abi-stap-; Armenian borrowed it as štapem 'I press', štap 'haste'. So this word does descend from *abi- = Ambhi — but through the root *stap 'to hasten, press' (PIE *step-, Pok. 1013), not through tap 'to be hot': Nourai's gloss 'in heat, in a hurry' is Horn's 1893 rationalisation of a wrong cut. Both words therefore reach the chart's root box, if at all, by a different road than drawn.

nodes.derivation: These are not Avestan words but Gershevitch's reconstructions in the Avestan Hymn to Mithra, p.220 n. (his index entry reads '*abi-dasta(na)-, 220 n.'). Reasoning: Pahlavi has abdast 'hand-guard' (MacKenzie ʾbdst'), and Gershevitch proposes that Pahl. *ʾwstnk / *ʾwystk should be read as *abistānak / *abistak going back to '*abi-sta-, amplified by -ka- and -na-ka-', and that '*abista(na)ka- … may be a reduction of *abi-d(a)sta-(na)ka-', comparing 'Yidgha avidasta "sleeve" < *uda-dasta- (Morgenstierne)' and 'Oss. fiston, Dig. fæstonæ "handle" < *pati-dastanæ, cf. Khot. dastāna "handle"'. The three shapes Nourai prints are Gershevitch's *abi-dasta-, a shortened *ā-dasta- and the still shorter *ā-d(a)st- (the chart's 'a-dsta' is Nourai's rendering of *ā-d(a)st-, not a scan error — the printed page reads 'a-dsta'). Second element dasta- 'hand' (PIE *ǵʰes-to-, Nourai's 'Ghesto'), first element the preverb abi-, so the formation would mean 'that which is over the hands'. Plausible, but reconstructed, and the box's language label 'Avestan' is wrong for a Middle-Iranian-based reconstruction.

W. Bailey took place in Oss. fiston, Dig. fæstonæ "handle" < *pati-dastanæ, cf. Khot. dastāna "handle" … Perhaps NPers. astīn "sleeve" similarly goes back to *ā-d(a)st-.' nodes.derivation: NP āstīn آستین 'sleeve', attested from Ferdowsī (c. 1010). Gershevitch's proposal, which Nourai follows, is āstīn < *ā-d(a)st(a)n- < *abi-dasta-na-, i.e. 'the (garment) over the hand', with loss of the intervocalic d in the reduced form and the -īn suffix; the parallel he cites is Ossetic fiston 'handle' < *pati-dastanæ beside Khotanese dastāna 'handle', and the type is supported by Middle Persian abdast 'hand-guard'. The competing modern view is Herzenberg's (2014, cited by Wiktionary): āstīn is a loan from a South-Eastern Iranian language, cf. Pashto lastúṇay 'sleeve' beside lās 'hand', with the *d- > l- shift of some Eastern Iranian languages and loss of the initial l- in Persian; Wiktionary flatly calls the word 'of unknown etymology due to not having any clear cognates'. Both proposals build the word on 'hand', so the semantics of Nourai's arrow are uncontroversial; the specific route through aiwi-/abi- is one scholar's conjecture, not a consensus.

nodes.derivation: OP abiy is the regular SW-Iranian reflex of PIE *m̥bʰi / *obhi: PII *Habʰí > OP abiy, used as a preposition with the accusative and as a verbal prefix (Bīsotūn passim: 'hauv … abiy avam ašiyava' 'he marched against him'; XPg 9 abiy-ajāvayam 'I added to'). 'abi' is not a separate word but the pre-consonantal sandhi variant of the same preverb, which Kent documents as a contraction of -iya- to -i-: 'abi-javayam, also abiy-ajāvayam'. 'abiš' is the -s extended adverbial form (Pokorny: 'über av. aibiš, apers. abiš strittiger Bed. s. Pedersen KZ 40, 127, Bartholomae IF 19, Beiheft S.106'), i.e. it is genuinely attested but its meaning has been argued over for a century. Nourai's gloss 'over, above' is only part of the picture: Kent's Lexicon gives 'to, against, in addition to'.

nodes.derivation: Gk. ἀμφί 'around, on both sides, about' is the direct reflex of full-grade *h₂m̥bʰi (Mycenaean a-pi already), with the by-form ἀμφίς 'on both sides' carrying the same adverbial -s as OP abiš; the related dual ἄμφω 'both' (< *h₂m̥bʰoh₁) gives ἀμφότερος. As a prefix ἀμφι- is fully productive in Greek and passes into the international vocabulary through Latin.

nodes.derivation: both: Middle English bathe/bothe, borrowed in the Viking age from Old Norse báðir (a compound of the inherited dual *bai 'both' with the demonstrative/article, cf. nodes.derivation: ambīre 'to go around' = ambi- (the Latin reflex of *h₂m̥bʰi, amb- before a vowel, am-/an- before a consonant) + īre 'to go' (PIE *h₁ey-, Nourai's 'Ei'); its participle ambiēns gives ambient and its noun ambitiō, ambitus 'a going round (canvassing for votes)' gives ambition. That half is straightforwardly Latin and confirmed. ambactus, however, is NOT a Latin formation: every authority makes it a Gaulish word taken into Latin. Festus glosses 'apud Ennium lingua gallica seruus appellatur … seruus ambactus, i.e. circumactus dicitur', Caesar uses it of Gauls (BG 6.15.2), and Ernout-Meillet call it 'Substitut gaulois de i.-e. *ambhi-'; Watkins files it under ag- as 'Celtic *amb(i)-ag-to-, "one sent around" (*ambi, around; see ambhi), in Latin ambactus, servant'. So the box is right about the morphology (*ambhi- + *ag- 'to drive') but wrong to label the word Latin — it is a Celtic compound that Latin (and, through Germanic, Romance) borrowed.

nodes.derivation: ambient: Lat. ambiēns, -entis, present participle of ambīre 'to go round, surround', into English in the 1590s. ambassador / embassy: Gaulish *ambaktos 'one sent around' > Latin ambactus 'vassal, servant'; borrowed into Germanic (Goth. andbahts 'servant', OHG ambaht, whence German Amt 'office'); Germanic *ambaht- 'service' was then re-borrowed into Gallo-Romance as Old Provençal *ambaissa 'service' > ambaissada, Italian ambasciata, whence Old French ambassee > English embassy (1570s) and Italian ambasciatore > Old French ambassadeur > Middle English ambassadour (late 14c.). The chain is thus Celtic → Latin → Germanic → Romance → English, a genuine round trip that the chart's single Latin → English arrow compresses.

nodes.derivation: This node is taken wholesale from Stuart Mann's Indo-European Comparative Dictionary, whose entry reads 'ambhor-, ambhr- (for ambh-bhor, -bhr-, cf. ambhō and bher-, bhor-) "two-handled vessel"', citing Skt. ambhṛṇaḥ, Gk. ἀμφορεύς / ἀμφιφορεύς, Lat. amphora, OHG ampri, OE amber/embren, Du. emmer, ON/Sw. ámbar. So the reconstruction is real and Nourai's page is right; the reservations are (i) the mainstream analysis of ἀμφορεύς is not *ambhō-bher- 'carried by both (hands)' but simply ἀμφι- + -φορεύς 'carrier around', the shorter ἀμφορεύς being a syncopated ἀμφιφορεύς already in Homer, so *ambhō- 'both' is Mann's own idea; (ii) Mann's dictionary is a lone, unreviewed reconstruction manual with no Pokorny or Walde-Pokorny entry behind this lemma; (iii) Mann glosses the etymon 'two-handled VESSEL', while Nourai converts it to 'a two-handled tool' to make it fit the pliers of node #20.

nodes.derivation: NP anbor / anbur انبر 'tongs, pliers' (with the by-forms انبره anbura and the compound انبردست anbor-dast). Moʿin defines it 'آلت فلزی دو شاخه که با آن آتش یا چیز دیگر را برگیرند' — 'a two-pronged metal implement with which one picks up fire or something else' — so Nourai's gloss and his extras انبره، انبردست are right. The DERIVATION is not. Mann's entry (node #19) does list 'Per. ambar' among the reflexes of *ambhor-, but in a list whose other members are ἀμφορεύς, amphora, OE amber, Du. emmer 'bucket' and Sw. ámbar, Mann's Persian item is plainly the vessel-word انبار anbār 'store, granary' — and Persian anbār is universally derived from Old Iranian *ham-pāra-/*ham-bāra- 'that which is heaped together' (ham- 'together' + bar- 'to carry'), the same prefix that gives انباشتن anbāštan 'to heap up' and انبوه anbūh 'crowd'. That native ham- > NP an-/am- is the obvious source of the an- of انبر too ('that which brings/holds together' — exactly a pair of tongs), and it has nothing to do with *ambhi/*ambhō. Wiktionary, the only modern reference to treat انبر, gives yet a third origin ('From Middle Iranian, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- "sharp"', unsourced). No independent authority supports Mann's *ambhō-bher- > Persian pliers, so the edge is disputed even though the word itself is well documented.

ref_check.note: IEC.txt leaf 25 s.v. ambhor-: the entry does read 'Per. ambar', but under the gloss 'two-handled vessel' and among amphora / OE amber / Du. emmer 'bucket'. Mann's 'ambar' is therefore the vessel-word انبار, not انبر 'pliers'; Nourai has re-pointed it.

Moʿin's page number could not be verified (only the unpaginated 2-vol abridgement is on disk), but the entry is there verbatim: 'انبر [= انبره] (اِ.) آلت فلزی دو شاخه که با آن آتش یا چیز دیگر را برگیرند … (مکن.) نوعی از اهرم که نیروی کارگر در وسط آن قرار دارد'; also 'انبردست' and 'انبره'. All three of Nourai's Persian forms and his gloss 'pliers' are Moʿin's; Moʿin supplies no etymology, so he does not support the arrow, only the word. Alphabetically انبر falls in the 360s of Moʿin vol. 1, so the page number is credible.
